title: I don’t know how to watch movies

commenti.body: Is this the case with all movies? It sounds to me like you’re watching stuff you don’t like. Think of some films that actually kept your attention, if any, find stuff in the same genre or things by the same director and see if that helps? You might just not be into films.

Congrats on being married.

If you think of movies like music ( which is something the well-regarded Stanley Kubrick has stated) there are many movies that won't ring true with how you experience them, but on the other side of the pole, films that you like are usually part of a greater genre, and so first thing to do would be to see what other films are in that same genre and how they relate to the film that one appreciates.

I do think analysis of themes and motifs or scenes are good for films that one has already seen, but I do think that trying to start the analytical process with a first-time film is the non-ideal way to do it.

Films are designed to produce emotions - so I think there shouldn't be anything inhibiting emotion when watching a film for the first time.

However I think film theory is a good way to create a plausible explanation to why one is able to experience such emotions.


I really think the book "Understanding film Theory", just hits it out of the park by not only showcasing several popular theoretical frameworks, but also showing an argument against those same ideas.

I like Cinema Tyler and Every frame a Painting for video essays, and Lindsay Ellis is very good, too.  

I hope this helps.

It really depends as there are so many different ways to make a film and tell a story, but like most forms of storytelling I think it's a great start to identify the theme. What is the writer/director really trying to talk about with this film, this scene, this line of dialogue, this cut, this camera move, etc.

 Assume most films are making some sort of statement, and remember that everything you are seeing and hearing is included in the film by choice. Even a theme as simple and universal as "good and evil" you can ask yourself "what is this moment telling me about the nature of good, or the nature of evil?" 

This doesn't really address the ability to be critical about movies but has been the most important part of me understanding and connecting with movies.
Thank you so much! That movie is definitely my introduction to that genre so I’m sure that’s a big part of it

Yeah, not with all movies.  Anything from Christopher Nolan, or mysterious circumstances that don’t quite line up until you start to see the unraveling. I have not enjoyed many movies as much The Prestige

I mean if you aren’t engaged by the movie it doesn’t mean you’re doing anything wrong, there’s certain movies that engage us and certain ones that don’t, regardless of how “good” they are. Taste is a thing and if you aren’t vibing with something then maybe you’re just learning about what you like and what you don’t. 

If you’re having a general issue with focusing on films, I feel your pain because I struggle with this even with movies I know that I like. Limiting distractions helps, I keep my phone away from me. Making sure you’re comfortable is good, have a good couch or bed to be sitting on. I recently got a pretty big tv which helps too, I can’t focus on stuff if the screen is small or if I’m watching on my laptop, I can’t even watch movies like that anymore. 

Also, I go to movie theaters a lot. I’m lucky to live in a large city that has a fair amount of indie theaters show all types of stuff including older classic films. I find I can focus way more at the cinema than I can at home, just by the nature of spending money and committing my time to being there, and the large screen and sound system. Not sure where you live but if you’re near a bigger city I would check out what your options are.

Well it’ll take a while to really build up a library or stuff you can compare too. Also you might be w at hung the wrong movies for the moment. Personally I wouldn’t start with the greats. I would just meander around. What types of movies do you like to watch?

I normally break up my movie watching to keep me engaged. Like I’ll do some old movies, then I’ll watch some action movies, then I’ll watch some foreign film, and maybe I’ll watch some comedy, and then maybe I finally feel like watching a Bergman. I owned stalker for 4 years before I finally felt ready to watch it. 

I could message you my letterbox’d so you get an idea. For example I just watched all the taken films, and Batman, and then I watched a Hitchcock.

Also in regards to being able to speak about the films clearly I think besides watching a big variety, is your check out some video essays on YouTube. Like if you find a movie you loved watch an essay on it. There are many aspects of a film too from camera angles to casting choices so there are so many things to talk about.


Eventually you will build up to tougher movies with a better attention span. 

What are some of your favorite. Another tip is to find directors you like and dig into their work.

Have you seen a lot of Wes anderson, Kubrick, and Scorsese?

There are movies that got me so bored that I just can't focus on the plot. Some of Christopher Nolan's movies, matrix part 2 and 3, lord of the ring, star wars. Lots of people loves those titles, but they are just not for me, even though I love cinema quite a lot.

What I believe can help you is to get more "movie educated". It looks like you are not being "stimulated" enough so that what you are watching is keeping your attention. Therefore introducing some thoughts such as "how did they do that", "did they use special effects or practical effects?", "why was this shot using this angle?" "who wrote the script, and why in that way?", why is this particular movie "the epitome of \_\_\_\_ genre?", "who did the sound, how does the sound add to the experience here?" etc.   
These are some examples of things to think about:  
\- Exploring Film Industries - Unveiling the Magic of Bollywood  
\- Unveiling Giallo Films: A Dive into Stylish Italian Thrillers  
\- Exploring Film Industries - The Enchanting World of Hong Kong Cinema  
\- Techniques in Cinema: The Intimate World of Close-Up Shots  
\- Techniques in Cinema: The Art of Tracking Shots  
\- Techniques in Cinema: Unleashing the Enchantment of Special Effects  
\- Techniques in Cinema: Painting with Color on the Silver Screen  
\- Techniques in Cinema: The Power of Sound in Film"  
\- Cinema Movements: The Adventurous World of Australian New Wave  
\- Cinematic Movements: The Liberation of French New Wave  
\- Cinematic Movements: The Revolution of New Hollywood  
\- Sci-Fi Odyssey: Unveiling the Wonders of the Genre  
\- Slash and Thrash: My Dive into the Thrilling World of Slasher Films  
\- The Evolution of Police Procedurals: A Cinematic Journey  
I think that the techniques might be of great benefit for you to dip your toes into the technicalities in a fun way, and then expand, while the other topics are a great way to make your brain start thinking in ways "movie guys" think which will both have a huge impact on your movie watching experience.  
I send these out for free weekly, covering these and many more, so if you think it might work for you feel free to join [here](https://cinneman.beehiiv.com/subscribe) & become cinema smarter while drinking coffee! It's free and if you don't like it just unsubscribe, no hard feelings:) I think these are a great way because even though books are the best, these are just so easy - you receive 5 min nuggets, and your brain soaks them up easily, so that you can notice what you learned on a Thursday, during a movie night on a Friday.

Look into more psychological thrillers and use that as your jumping off point, then if it’s a film you enjoyed look up other stuff the director made in a different genre and see if that sticks, and if it doesn’t, oh well, it’s okay to not like something, you shouldn’t be forcing yourself to.
